                JOHN BURROW'S COMMENTS REGARDING REMAND ON
                      PRELIMINARY ORDER ISSUES 11 AND 13
TO THE HONORABLE ADMINISTRATIVE LAW JUDGES AND COMMISSIONERS:
     John Burrow, Pro Se Intervenor, Bell County Landowner, respectfully files this response
to Chairman Gleeson's memorandum dated September 9,2026 regarding remand of State
Office of Administrative Hearings (SOAH) Administrative Law Judges' (ALJs') Proposal For
Decision (PFD) on Preliminary Order Issues 11 and 13.
    John Burrow supports the ALJ's original recommendation to deny the Import Path 2
applications, Dockets 59182 and 59475. The central question remains: did the Applicants
prove that Import Path 2 is necessary to satisfy a state or federal reliability standard? The
answer is no.
    The Permian Basin Reliability Plan (PBRP) showed that ERCOT identified reliability
concerns in the Permian Basin region only and used NERC planning criteria while modeling
solutions. This does not prove that Import Path 2 importing electricity from a totally different
area of the state to a specific region is required by NERC. The PBRP separates local
Permian Basin reliability needs from regional statewide import needs. It does not show that
Import Path 2 is necessary to satisfy any NERC violations. The PBRP was modeled from
inconsistent load and generation assumptions. A model that does not represent the future
ERCOT statewide grid system cannot establish that Import Path 2 is federally required.

I. THE SIMPLE ANSWER TO ISSUE 11 IS: IMPORT PATH 2 WAS NOT PROVEN
NECESSARY TO MEET NERC STANDARDS
     Preliminary Order Issue 11 asks whether the proposed facilities are necessary to meet
state or federal reliability standards. The word necessary matters. The question is not
whether a system containing Import Path 2 can meet NERC criteria. The question is whether
NERC compliance requires Import Path 2.

                                              Page 1
      That distinction is important because the PBRP and Applicants repeatedly move between
three different ideas as if they mean the same thing: (1) ERCOT performed studies using
NERC criteria; (2) a proposed system configuration meets NERC criteria; and (3) Import Path
2 is necessary to meet NERC criteria. They are not the same. The first describes the study
method. The second describes a result under selected assumptions. Only the third would
answer Preliminary Order Issue 11.
     The ALJs already recognized the project specific problem. The PFD found that NERC
may influence ERCOT's regional planning, but they do not substitute for proof that Import
Path 2 itself is independently needed. The PFD also found that Applicants did not perform a
partial build study establishing the independent need for Import Path 2 and did not establish
that Import Path 2 is needed in 2030. Those are finding of facts and conclusion of law
establish at the hearing on merits, written testimony, and evidence. It is clear, Import Path 2
was not proven to be needed.
Il. THE PBRP MODEL CANNOT BE USED AS RELIABLE PROOF THAT IMPORT PATH 2
IS REQUIRED BY NERC TPL-001-5.1
A. NERC TPL-001 requires the planning model to represent projected system
conditions
    NERC TPL-001-5.1 is a transmission planning standard. Its modeling requirements are
important here. The standard requires Planning Coordinators and Transmission Planners
(ERCOT and the Applicants) to maintain system models for planning studies that represent
projected system conditions, including real and planned load and generation forecasts. It
requires the planning assessment must use proven and accurate current and/or past studies
and document assumptions and the results of the model or models. From TPL-001-5.1, a
certain level of accuracy is the representation of a power system, the data submitted must be
correct, periodically checked, and updated. It also states that one set of data that changes
on a more frequent basis is load data, and updates to load data are needed when new
improved forecast are created.
    Every planning disagreement does not automatically become a NERC violation while not
any party can label NERC TPL-001 as proof of federal necessity while ignoring whether the
model used to reach the conclusion represented the current and future grid conditions. In this
case, the applicant is introducing a regional Permian Basin requirement that requires a
statewide solution. If a regional grid model is materially incomplete or inconsistent and
doesn't include statewide grid load and demand, the resulting model cannot be proof that
Import Path 2 is required for NERC compliance.
B. ERCOT used materially different future system assumptions in the PBRP and the
contemporaneous 2024 RTP
    ERCOT developed the PBRP and the 2024 Regional Transmission Plan at the same
time, but the two studies did not use the same load and generation assumptions for 2030
Texas. The PBRP began with the 2023 RTP and selectively added newer Transmission
Service Provider (TSP) provided load in the Permian Basin. At the same time, ERCOT
acknowledged the 2024 RTP identified approximately 59,400 MW of additional demand
across the grid needed by 2030.


                                             Page 2
      Kennedy's filings identify discrepancies in generation assumptions. The PBRP added
approximately 17,170 MW of future generation, while the contemporaneous 2024 RTP
included approximately 59,200 MW. That difference is 42,000 MW. The point is not that
generation must always be identical between two studies. The point is that these enormous
differences show that ERCOT was using different future load and generation conditions while
modeling the same future ERCOT grid. This should be of concern.
    Bottom line, ERCOT modeled two different 2030 Texas grids. The PBRP model
concentrated newer load and not all planned generation in the Permian region while the 2024
RTP incorporated a much larger statewide future load and generation. Those two models can
produce very different answers about where electricity is available, where it is needed, and
how much can transfer from east to west.
C. The PBRP's asymmetric load and generation inputs could create the very east to
west transfer the study later claimed was needed
   Models respond to the numbers that are inputted. If a model input locates a very large
new demand in West Texas, leaves substantial newer demand outside the Permian out of the
model, and adds substantial future generation in Central and East Texas, the model will
naturally show power moving from the apparent surplus area toward the apparent deficit
area.
    This would appear the model was intentionally manipulated. It shows why the result must
be tested using consistent and accurate future load and generation. Without this, it cannot be
relied upon especially to condemn thousands of acres of private property for a massive, long
haul transmission corridor. If you input certain assumptions, exclude others, or change the
inputs until a model produces an answer you want, that isn't an outcome from a model. That's
modeling an outcome.
    The problem becomes especially significant for Bell County East. ERCOT's 2024 and
2025 RTP identified substantial increase in load in the Central Texas region. A model that
treats Central Texas as a major source for exporting power west cannot be valid. This
reconciliation was not performed in the PBRP and the ALJ's are correct that the applicants
evidence used to justify Import Path 2 was not proven.
D. The PBRP base cases were initially unsolvable and were iteratively modified
    The PBRP (section 4, Reliability Need, page 15) indicates the initial 2030 and 2038
power flow were not solvable within the Permian Region. ERCOT then modeled by adding
load incrementally, then identify violations, then added local transmission, and then repeated
the process. The PBRP is a planning exercise identifying areas of concern and possible
solutions. The ERCOT model used to develop the PBRP study, modeled all three import
paths combined as it was assumed all three import paths were needed. This is inherently
wrong and does not follow typical engineer modeling. EROCT then reported it would meet
NERC reliability criteria, but the PBRP does not document that removing Import Path 2 would
result in failure. It is a faulty assumption that all import paths are needed. This does not offer
project specific proof that NERC TPL-001-5.1 specifically requires Import Path 2. In addition,
the applicants identified 5 individual CCN applications as separate stand-alone projects, yet
they will argue the PPRP and NERC as the justification that ALL import paths are needed to
solve Permian Basin power flow issues and compliance with federal requirements. This just

                                              Page 3
 doesn't make logical sense. If this was the case, all 5 projects should have been submitted
as an individual CCN application.
Ill. THE PBRP IDENTIFIES LOCAL RELIABILITY VIOLATIONS AND LOCAL UPGRADES;
IT DOES NOT SAY IMPORT PATH 2 IS NECESSARY TO CORRECT A SPECIFIC NERC
VIOLATION
     What the PBRP states or how it is structured matters. Its reliability needs identify thermal,
voltage, and stability problems within the Permian region only, not statewide or other Texas
regions. It discusses local transmission upgrades needed to serve those loads within the
Permian Basin region. The PBRP then separately evaluates import needs and alternative
import paths to increase transfer capability into the region.
     That distinction is exactly what Preliminary Order Issue 11 requires the ALJs to examine.
If a local transmission or distribution line or other local upgrade is identified as required or
necessary to correct a specific thermal or voltage violation, that is a direct reliability need.
Import Path 2 is different. The PBRP describes import capability as needed to serve
specifically assumed forecasted demand, it does not identify a specific NERC requirement
that says Import Path 2 must be constructed, nor does it show that NERC compliance fails
unless Import Path 2 is built.
    The PBRP structure supports the ALJs' original recommendations. Evidence that local
Permian Basin upgrades are necessary under NERC criteria does not automatically prove
that Import Path 2 beginning in Central Texas is necessary under NERC.

IV. 'MEETS NERC' DOES NOT MEAN 'REQUIRED BY NERC'
    PBRP Table E 1 or statement saying a 765 kV import path meets NERC reliability criteria
does not prove Import Path 2 is required for NERC compliance. Example: A new four lane
bridge may meet every federal safety standard. That does not mean federal safety standards
require the bridge to be built. To prove necessity, it must be shown the applicable standard
cannot be satisfied without that bridge.
    The same logic applies here. The Applicants must identify the NERC or state reliability
requirement, identify the violation or deficiency, and connect that requirement to Import Path
2 with evidence showing that Import Path 2 is necessary. The evidentiary record does not
indicate that the PBRP does not comply with NERC if Import Path 2 is not constructed.

V. IMPORT PATH 2 IS A STATEWIDE TRANSFER SOLUTION, SO ITS NEED CANNOT
BE RELIABLY DETERMINED FROM A PERMIAN BASIN REGIONALLY UPDATED LOAD
MODEL
    The PBRP was directed at reliability needs in the Permian Basin region. That regional
focus may make sense for identifying local facilities inside the Permian. Import Path 2 is not a
local Permian transmission line. It is a transmission line intended to move power from Bell
County and Central Texas across a large part of Texas.
    Every import has an export. To determine whether the Permian must import power from
Central Texas, ERCOT must reasonably model both ends. That means Bell County and
Central Texas matters just as much as Permian Basin region. If Central Texas has tens of
thousands of megawatts of newer forecast load that are not reflected in the PBRP
assumptions, the model will overstate how much power is available to export west.
                                               Page 4
     Once ERCOT used the PBRP to recommend a path that reaches far outside the Permian
Basin and relies upon power transfers across the ERCOT system, the import analysis
became a statewide power flow question. A specifically picked regional load placed into the
2023 RTP is not a reliable substitute for a contemporaneous statewide load and generation
forecast used in the 2024 RTP. Again, this is not an outcome from a model, its modeling an
outcome.
VI. THE PBRP DOES NOT SATISFY THE APPLICANTS' BURDEN OF PROOF FOR
IMPORT PATH 2
     The Applicants, not ERCOT and not the ALJs, carry the burden to prove the CCN
application. Referring repeatedly to the PBRP does not justify project specific evidence
presented during this process. Before Import Path 2 can be to be required, the record should
answer basic questions: how much power must transfer thru Import Path 2; where will the
power come from; whether Bell County and Central Texas will actually have the power to
serve its own future load; when the power is needed; what specific NERC or state reliability
violation requires the power; and why Import Path 2 is necessary to resolve that violation.
    The ALJs found those answers were not established. Reopening the record should not
be necessary. The applicant has the burden of proof and the ALJ's determined they didn't
prove need. Just because the findings of facts and conclusion of law didn't produce the
applicants desired result should not allow them additional time and means to change the
narrative and outcome.
VII. ISSUE 13 DOES NOT CORRECT THE FAILURE TO PROVE RELIABILITY NEED
     Preliminary Order Issue 13 asks for the estimated congestion cost savings to consumers
that may result from the proposed facilities. Chairman Gleeson's memorandum recognizes
that the PFD found Applicants did not submit evidence regarding estimated congestion cost
savings. That is an answer supported by the record: the savings were not proven.
   The applicants should not be giving the opportunity to reposition Import Path 2 as an
economic project after presenting it as a reliability project. The absence of congestion cost
evidence at the hearing should not be converted into an opportunity to build a new economic
case after the PFD.

Vlll. THE REMAND SHOULD NOT BECOME A SECOND CHANCE TO REPAIR THE
APPLICANTS' CASE
    Chairman Gleeson's memorandum expressly states that he does not know whether
reopening the record is necessary and would defer that decision to the ALJs. This is
important. The applicants knew Preliminary Order Issues 11 and 13 before the hearing. They
selected their witnesses, offered their studies, conducted discovery, presented evidence, and
briefed need.
    The ALJs should not reopen the case and allow additional evidence. The ALJ's should
not permit Applicants to replace the PBRP with a new study, create a new project-specific
NERC analysis that did not exist at the hearing, or add new congestion cost calculations to
change a failure of proof. The case should be decided on whether the application was

                                             Page 5
 proven, not on whether a stronger case can be assembled after the Applicants learned why
the ALJs recommended denial.

IX. FINDINGS IN EVIDENTIARY SUPPORT FOR THE ALJS
1. NERC TPL-001-5.1 establishes transmission system planning performance requirements
   and requires planning models to represent updated and accurate system conditions,
   including load forecasts and generation required for load.
2. The PBRP used NERC TPL-001-5.1 and ERCOT planning criteria as part of its planning
   methodology, but use of those criteria does not establish that Import Path 2 is necessary
   to comply with NERC.
3. The PBRP began with the 2023 RTP case and incorporated some specific but not all TSP
   load and generation forecasts within the Permian Basin, while ERCOT
   contemporaneously recognized substantially greater additional statewide load and
   generation across the ERCOT grid in the 2024 RTP.
4. The PBRP and 2024 RTP used materially different future load-and-generation
   assumptions for the same future planning horizon, including approximately 17,170 MW of
   added future generation in the PBRP versus approximately 59,200 MW in the 2024 RTP.
5. Because the amount and direction of modeled power transfers depend upon the
   geographic relationship between generation and load, materially inconsistent Bell County
   and Permian Basin Region load and generation assumptions will materially affect the
   need for Import Path 2.
6. Import Path 2 is intended to transfer power across the ERCOT system from Central Texas
   toward the Permian Basin and therefore depends upon grid wide source and destination
   conditions, not only load conditions within the Permian Basin.
7. The PBRP identifies reliability local transmission upgrades to address thermal, voltage,
   stability, and load-serving needs within the Permian Basin.
8. The PBRP does not establish that Import Path 2 is required to correct an identified NERC
   TPL-001-5.1 violation or that NERC compliance cannot be achieved without Import Path
   2.
9. A finding that an import path meets NERC reliability criteria is not equivalent to a finding
   that Import Path 2 is necessary and required to meet NERC reliability criteria.
10. Applicants did not establish a project specific, quantifiable reliability need for Import Path
   2 independent of the broader PBRP import-path strategy.
11. Applicants did not quantify estimated congestion cost savings attributable to Import Path
   2 in the evidentiary record considered by the PFD.
12. The evidence therefore does not establish a yes answer to Preliminary Order Issue 11 or
   a yes answer to Preliminary Order Issue 13 indicating Import Path 2 is required.
X. REQUESTED CONCLUSION
     After addressing Preliminary Order Issues 11 and 13, request the ALJs adhere to their
original recommendation to deny the Import Path 2 applications. The evidence may have
established the Permian Basin has substantial reliability and load growth concerns. It does
not establish that NERC requires Import Path 2, and it does not establish that the PBRP's
                                              Page 6
 materially inconsistent future system model can be relied upon as project-specific proof of
federal reliability necessity.
    A reliability standard is not a blank check for a transmission project. The Applicants must
prove the connection between the standard, the violation, and the specific facilities they ask
the State to approve. They did not do that here.
PRAYER
     WHEREFORE, PREMISES CONSIDERED, John Burrow respectfully requests that the
ALJs expressly answer Preliminary Order Issue 11 by finding that Applicants failed to prove
Import Path 2 is necessary to meet state or federal reliability standards; answer Preliminary
Order Issue 13 by finding that Applicants failed to provide reliable quantified congestion cost
savings attributable to Import Path 2; give the PBRP no controlling or dispositive weight as
proof of Import Path 2 project NERC necessity; and adhere to the original recommendation
that the Import Path 2 applications be denied.
